surveyDefinition.title: Running Shoes — consumer survey (Global)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 5 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, price sensitivity, and sustainability orientation.

segments.name: Performance-Focused Runners
segments.description: High-frequency runners (4+ times per week) who train for races or personal bests. They prioritize cushioning, stability, weight, and durability over price, and are willing to pay $150+ for the right shoe. They research extensively and are loyal to brands that deliver performance.

segments.name: Value-Driven Joggers
segments.description: Run 1-3 times per week for fitness or stress relief. They are price-sensitive and often abandon purchases above $100. They seek comfort and durability at a reasonable price, and are open to switching brands for better value. They buy on sale or from discount retailers.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Committed Buyers
segments.description: Run regularly and are strongly motivated by sustainability. They are willing to pay a premium for eco-friendly materials and transparent claims, but are frustrated by the lack of affordable options. They research brand sustainability practices and prioritize recycled or carbon-neutral products.

segments.name: Style-Led Casual Users
segments.description: Run occasionally (less than once a week) but wear running shoes for daily casual use. They prioritize aesthetics, brand image, and comfort for all-day wear. They are moderately price-sensitive and often buy lifestyle-oriented models that look good on and off the run.

segments.name: Comfort-Seeking Recreational Buyers
segments.description: Run or walk for recreation, often older or injury-prone. They prioritize cushioning, arch support, and fit over speed or style. They are willing to pay for comfort but are frustrated by inconsistent sizing and lack of options for specific foot types. They value in-store fitting and expert advice.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Running Shoes buyers worldwide. It asks how people use Running Shoes, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories. This global view is not a separate fieldwork exercise: it selects the strongest questions from the regional surveys and blends their percentages using population-style regional weights.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults worldwide who buy or use Running Shoes for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Adults who run for exercise, sport, or recreation; Purchased or intend to purchase running shoes within the last/next 12 months; Involved in the purchase decision (either self-buy or primary influencer). Excluded: Professional athletes whose shoes are provided by sponsors; Children under 18 (unless purchasing for themselves, but typically parent decides); People who only wear running shoes as casual fashion without running.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for themselves, pay at retail or online, and decide based on fit, brand, and price. While some businesses may purchase for employees, the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
respondentBehaviours: Engages in running or jogging at least once a week
Purchases athletic footwear at least once a year
Researches online reviews or seeks recommendations before buying
Values performance features (cushioning, stability, weight) or lifestyle aesthetics
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Running Activity & Usage Context
sections.covers: Establishes who runs, how often, where, and for what purpose, to segment by engagement and need state.

sections.label: Purchase Journey & Decision Drivers
sections.covers: Covers the triggers, research, channels, spend, and decision factors behind buying running shoes.

sections.label: Fit, Performance & Product Requirements
sections.covers: Explores must-have features, quality cues, sustainability expectations, and trade-offs in shoe design and price.

sections.label: Satisfaction & Replacement Intent
sections.covers: Measures satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, and future purchase/replacement plans.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's running identity — how often, where, and why they run — which immediately separates casual joggers from committed athletes. It then walks through the purchase journey, from what triggers a new pair to where they buy and what they pay, revealing price sensitivity and channel preferences. Next, it drills into product requirements, forcing trade-offs between performance, comfort, style, and sustainability, which distinguishes the eco-conscious from the performance-driven. Finally, it measures satisfaction and future intent, capturing pain points…

questions.question: In a typical week, how many times do you run?
questions.insight: Top response: 1–2 times a week (34.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Style-Led Casual Users and Comfort-Seeking Recreational Buyers pull the low-frequency end; Performance-Focused Runners and Eco-Conscious Committed Buyers concentrate at the high-frequency end.

questions.question: How long have you been running or jogging regularly?
questions.insight: Top response: More than 5 years (34.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Value-Driven Joggers and Style-Led Casual Users skew to shorter tenure; Performance-Focused Runners and Comfort-Seeking Recreational Buyers are more experienced.

options: On a treadmill or indoor track

data.label: On a treadmill or indoor track

questions.insight: Top response: On roads or sidewalks (45.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Road running dominates across most segments; Trail-oriented personas and Performance-Focused Runners drive the trail and mix-surface responses.

questions.question: What is the main reason you run?
options: Training for a race or event

data.label: Training for a race or event

questions.insight: Top response: General fitness and health (42.00%).
questions.distributionNote: General fitness dominates across most segments; Stress relief is strong among Corporate Wellness and Eco-Conscious segments.

questions.question: In the last 30 days, how many miles have you run in total?
questions.insight: Top response: 11–25 miles (34.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Value-Driven Joggers and Style-Led Casual Users cluster in the lower mileage bands.

options: Training for a marathon or longer event

data.label: Training for a marathon or longer event

questions.insight: Top response: Staying active and healthy (40.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Staying active is the top goal for Value-Driven Joggers and Comfort-Seeking Recreational Buyers.

questions.insight: Top response: My current pair is worn out or uncomfortable (48.00%).

questions.question: How much time did you spend researching before buying your last pair of running shoes?
questions.insight: Top response: 30 minutes to 1 hour (30.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Value-Driven Joggers and Comfort-Seeking Recreational Buyers skew to shorter research windows; Performance-Focused Runners and Eco-Conscious Committed Buyers spend more time verifying fit and sustainability claims.

questions.question: Where do you usually look for information before buying running shoes?
options: I usually don't research before buying

data.label: I usually don't research before buying

questions.insight: Top response: Online reviews and ratings (78.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Online reviews dominate across all segments; Performance-Focused Runners and Eco-Conscious Committed Buyers also rely on brand sites and expert fitting, while Style-Led Casual Users lean more on social media and friends.

questions.question: Where do you usually buy your running shoes?
questions.insight: Top response: Online specialist retailer (30.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Performance-Focused and Eco-Conscious buyers favor specialty and brand-direct channels; Value-Driven and Comfort-Seeking buyers are more likely to use department or mass retailers for price and convenience.

questions.question: How often do you buy a new pair of running shoes?
questions.insight: Top response: About once a year (32.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Performance-Focused Runners replace more frequently; Value-Driven and Style-Led users stretch replacement cycles to save money or because they use shoes casually.

questions.question: How would you describe the price range you usually pay for a new pair of running shoes?
questions.insight: Top response: $100 to $149 (35.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Performance-Focused and Eco-Conscious buyers are more willing to pay $100-$149, with a smaller premium tail above $150.

questions.question: Which of the following mattered most when you chose your last pair of running shoes?
questions.insight: Top response: Comfort and cushioning (28.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Comfort is the top priority across all segments.

questions.question: Which features would you refuse to give up in a running shoe?
options: Cushioning that feels comfortable on long runs
Durable sole that doesn't wear out quickly
Arch support that fits my foot type

questions.insight: Top response: Cushioning that feels comfortable on long runs (72.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Cushioning and durable soles are near-universal must-haves; Comfort-Seeking and Performance-Focused buyers also demand arch support, while Style-Led users are less likely to insist on any single feature.

questions.question: What would you be willing to pay more for in a running shoe?

questions.distributionNote: Value-Driven Joggers and Comfort-Seeking Recreational Buyers focus on sole firmness and cushioning response; Performance-Focused Runners and Style-Led Casual Users weigh lightness and support; stitching is a quality cue across segments.

questions.insight: Top response: The feel of the cushioning (38.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Comfort-Seeking Recreational Buyers and Value-Driven Joggers prioritize cushioning feel; Style-Led Casual Users drive look/color; Performance-Focused Runners and Eco-Conscious Committed Buyers split between weight, materials, and sustainability.

questions.question: Which width and size options do you need in a running shoe?
questions.insight: Top response: Half sizes (62.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Half sizes are a near-universal need across all segments; wide widths are particularly important to Comfort-Seeking Recreational Buyers and Value-Driven Joggers; extended sizes and kids' sizes are niche but present among family-oriented and taller runners.

questions.question: Which sustainability claims would make you more likely to buy a running shoe?

questions.distributionNote: Eco-Conscious Committed Buyers strongly drive recycled materials and transparency; other segments show moderate interest in carbon-neutral and biodegradable claims, while a substantial share of Value-Driven and Comfort-Seeking buyers remain indifferent.

questions.question: If you had to choose, which would you give up first in a running shoe?

segmentModel.tie_break: The question cp2 (typical weekly running frequency) is the most direct behavioural self-report and should settle ties, because it cleanly separates high-frequency performance runners (5+ times), moderate value joggers (1-2 times), and occasional style-led users (less than once a week).
notes: Eco-conscious segment is reachable via pe2, pe6, pe7, sf3, sf5, bb8.
Comfort-seeking segment is reachable via bb2, bb3, bb5, pe1, pe2, pe4, pe5, sf3, sf4, sf5.
Style-led segment is reachable via cp2, cp5, cp6, bb1, bb2, bb8, pe4, pe7.
Value-driven segment is reachable via cp2, cp5, cp6, bb1, bb2, bb4, bb5, bb7, bb8, sf5.
Performance-focused segment is reachable via cp2, cp5, cp6, cp7, bb1, bb3, bb4, bb5, bb7, pe1, pe2, pe4, sf5.
7 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=250 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.
